g12-history-uh1-t1.overview: Capitalism is the economic system of private ownership, profit and free markets that matured in Northwestern Europe between the 16th and 17th centuries. This lesson sets out its main features and the opposing critique of Karl Marx.
objectives: Describe the origins of capitalism after the breakup of feudalism
Explain mercantilism and why it declined in the 18th century
List the main characteristic features of capitalism
Summarise Adam Smith's classical doctrine of laissez-faire
Explain the main ideas of Marxian economics and its critique of capitalism
g12-history-uh1-t1.simple: Capitalism is an economic system built on private ownership of the means of production, profit and free markets. Many historians agree that fully fledged capitalism emerged in Northwestern Europe, especially Great Britain and the Netherlands, between the 16th and 17th centuries, when mercantilism flourished. Mercantilism means buying goods at one price and selling them at a higher price for profit. In the 18th century Adam Smith (1723-1790) challenged mercantilism in The Wealth of Nations (1776) and argued for laissez-faire, the idea that markets work best without government interference. Capitalism split society into the owning capitalist class and the wage-earning working class. Karl Marx attacked the system, called the exploitation of surplus value its main flaw, and predicted a workers' revolution.
g12-history-uh1-t1.detailed:
From feudalism to capitalism. Capitalism grew in the womb of decaying feudalism and has become the dominant economic system in the Western world since the breakup of feudalism. Many historians agree that fully fledged capitalism emerged in Northwestern Europe, especially in Great Britain and the Netherlands, from the 16th to the 17th centuries, when mercantilism was established.

Mercantilism. Mercantilism is defined as the distribution of goods that are bought at a certain price and sold at a higher price in order to generate profits. The ethics fostered by the Protestant Reformation of the 16th century helped consolidate capitalism, and the rise of strong nation states in Europe supported it through regulations, uniform monetary systems and public investment, eventually making possible the shift from public to private initiative.

The challenge from Adam Smith. In the 18th century mercantilism declined when a group of economic theorists led by Adam Smith challenged mercantilist doctrines. They believed that a state could only increase its wealth at the expense of another state's wealth while the amount of the world's wealth remained constant. As mercantilism declined, industrial capitalism arose in the mid-18th century because of the vast accumulation of capital during the phase of merchant capitalism and its investment in machinery. Industrial capitalism marked the development of the manufacturing factory system and led to the global domination of the capitalist mode of production.

Main features. Capitalism is characterised by private ownership of the means of production, especially in the industrial sector, where individuals and corporations own and operate companies and make decisions on the use of resources. Capitalist society was characterised by a split between two antagonistic classes: the capitalist class, which owned the means of production such as property, plants and equipment, and the working class, which sold its labour to the capitalist class in exchange for wages. Unlike previous systems, capitalism used accumulated capital to enlarge productive capacity rather than to invest in economically unproductive enterprises such as pyramids and cathedrals, and the motive for all companies was to make and sell goods and services only for profits.

Laissez-faire. Capitalist societies believe markets should be left alone to operate without government intervention, an idea known as laissez-faire. True capitalists believe a free market will always create the right amount of supply to meet demand and that all prices will adjust accordingly. The ideology of classical capitalism was articulated by Adam Smith (1723-1790) in his book An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776); this Scottish economist and moral philosopher is considered one of the forefathers of capitalism and recommended leaving economic decisions to the free play of self-regulating market forces.

Marxian economics. The growth of industrial capitalism in the 19th century created a vast new class of industrial workers whose generally miserable conditions inspired the revolutionary philosophy of Karl Marx. In the socialist system he described there was no private ownership: all means of production were collective or state-owned, and central planning determined how much should be produced and how all resources were allocated.

The Marxist critique. Marxian economics, named after Karl Marx, is the antithesis of capitalism. Marx believed that capitalism brings about class segregation between the capitalist class and the working class, and he called the exploitation of the surplus value of labour one of its major drawbacks. He argued that capitalist economies would weaken in systematic crises, that these crises would cause social disturbance, and that wealth would become concentrated in the hands of an even more privileged class. He predicted the inevitable overthrow of capitalism in a proletarian-led class war.

The distribution of goods that are bought at a certain price and sold at a higher price in order to generate profits.
The idea that markets should be left alone to operate without government intervention, since a free market supplies the right amount to meet demand.
The property, plants and equipment used to produce goods, owned in capitalism by individuals or corporations.
The owning class that owned the means of production and employed wage labour.
The class that owned only its labour power and sold it to the capitalist class in exchange for wages.

workedExamples.problem: According to Adam Smith, why should governments leave markets alone?
workedExamples.given: Smith argued in The Wealth of Nations (1776) for laissez-faire and the free play of self-regulating market forces.
workedExamples.formula: Historical skill: explaining an idea in the terms used by the author who wrote it.
workedExamples.substitution: Laissez-faire holds that a free market creates the right amount of supply to meet demand and that all prices adjust accordingly.
workedExamples.calculation: If markets regulate themselves, government intervention is unnecessary and may harm the general welfare Smith wanted to promote.
workedExamples.answer: Because self-regulating markets balance supply and demand, which Smith believed benefited practitioners while promoting society's general welfare.

workedExamples.problem: How did Marx explain the origin of profit in a wage labour contract?
workedExamples.given: Workers possess capital in the form of their labour, sell it under wage contracts and use their earnings for necessities, while the employer also earns a profit from the worker's labour.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: surplus value, the value the worker produces beyond the wage received.
workedExamples.substitution: The worker is paid a wage but produces more value than that wage.
workedExamples.calculation: The difference between the value produced and the wage paid is the surplus value, which the employer takes as profit.
workedExamples.answer: Marx argued that profit comes from the exploitation of the surplus value of the worker's labour.

workedExamples.problem: A country takes all factories into state ownership and plans output centrally. Which system described in the lesson does this match?
workedExamples.given: There is no private ownership; all means of production are collective or state-owned; central planning decides production and allocation.
workedExamples.formula: Historical comparison: distinguishing capitalism from the socialist system that Marx described.
workedExamples.substitution: Private ownership and the profit motive are absent and are replaced by collective ownership and planning.
workedExamples.calculation: Removing private ownership and market decisions matches Marx's socialist system, which the lesson calls the antithesis of capitalism.
workedExamples.answer: It matches the socialist system described by Marx, the opposite of capitalism.

workedExamples.problem: Why do many historians date fully fledged capitalism to the 16th and 17th centuries?
workedExamples.given: Fully fledged capitalism emerged in Northwestern Europe, especially Great Britain and the Netherlands, from the 16th to the 17th centuries when mercantilism was established.
workedExamples.formula: Historical skill: using a periodisation that the textbook provides.
workedExamples.substitution: The establishment of mercantilism and the support of strong nation states mark the maturing of capitalism.
workedExamples.calculation: If capitalism matured at the same time as mercantilism in those centuries, then the 16th and 17th centuries are the accepted starting point.
workedExamples.answer: Because that is when mercantilism was established and capitalism became fully fledged in Great Britain and the Netherlands.

commonMistakes: Confusing mercantilism, which buys and resells goods for profit, with laissez-faire, which opposes government interference in markets.
Thinking Adam Smith supported state control of the economy rather than the free play of market forces.
Believing capitalism appeared only in the 19th century and ignoring its 16th and 17th century roots.
Mixing up the capitalist class, which owns the means of production, with the working class, which sells its labour.
Treating Marxian economics as a defence of capitalism instead of its antithesis.
Forgetting that capitalism invested accumulated capital in productive capacity, not in unproductive monuments such as pyramids and cathedrals.
applications: Explaining to a classmate why a privately owned factory and a state-owned factory belong to different economic systems.
Debating in class the motion that free markets or state planning better serve ordinary people.
Linking Adam Smith's laissez-faire to present-day debates about how far government should regulate business in Ethiopia.
Reading a news report about a new investment and deciding who owns the means of production.
Comparing the working conditions described by Marx with conditions that workers still face today.
Using the idea of surplus value to discuss why the wage a worker receives can differ from the value produced.
g12-history-uh1-t1.summary: Capitalism is an economic system founded on private ownership of the means of production, the profit motive and laissez-faire, and it matured in Northwestern Europe in the 16th and 17th centuries under mercantilism. Adam Smith articulated its classical ideology in The Wealth of Nations (1776), while Karl Marx attacked it, pointing to class segregation, the exploitation of surplus value and an eventual revolution. Capitalism divided society into owners and wage workers and spread until it became the dominant economic system in the world.

g12-history-uh1-t2.overview: The Industrial Revolution was the first establishment of industrial capitalism in any country and took place in Britain between about 1750 and 1850. This lesson explains the factory system, steam power and railways, and the deep economic, social and political changes that followed.
objectives: Explain what the Industrial Revolution was and where it began
Describe the change from the putting out system to the factory system
Trace the development of steam power and the first railways
Analyse the economic results of the Industrial Revolution, including overproduction
Explain the social and political results, including the rise of new classes
g12-history-uh1-t2.simple: The Industrial Revolution was the first establishment of industrial capitalism in any country, and it took place in Britain between 1750/1780 and 1850. Production moved from small units under the old putting out system to the new factory system, where many wage workers laboured in large factories owned by industrial capitalists. Machines and steam power replaced hand work. Newcomen built the first commercially viable steam engine around 1705/1709, and James Watt in 1783/84 made a more powerful engine for factories. The Liverpool and Manchester railway opened in 1830. Cheap mass production led to overproduction, cities grew, agriculture became less dominant, and new classes of industrial bourgeoisie and proletariat appeared. Industry also made the West far more powerful than non-western states.
g12-history-uh1-t2.detailed:
What it was. The Industrial Revolution was the first establishment of industrial capitalism in any country, and it took place in Britain in the period between 1750/1780 and 1850. It was preceded by a long period of change going back at least to the mid-16th century and even to the Middle Ages, and change did not cease in the 1850s because industrialisation was a continuing process. By 1850 Britain was already a mature industrial state whose major industries and transport system had been transformed by machinery and steam power.

The factory system. Industrial production in major industries was transformed so that far greater and cheaper production became possible than ever before. This cheap mass production was achieved by interconnecting organisational and technological changes. Production moved from dispersed small units under the old putting out system to the new factory system, in which production was concentrated in large factories that employed many workers each. The industrial capitalist owned the factory and built the machinery, while the workers owned only their labour power, which they sold for money wages and which could be hired and dismissed at the will of the capitalist. By 1850 the factory system was dominant in major British industries, especially the cotton textile industry of Lancashire in the northwest of England.

Steam power. The new machines in factories employed inanimate power. Water and wind power had been used since the Middle Ages, but as the economy expanded and industry needed a form of power greater than water could provide and more flexible than waterpower, steam power came into use. The heat to generate steam came from burning coal, which in Britain was cheap and abundant. The first commercially viable steam engine was constructed by Newcomen around 1705/1709, but it could be used only for pumps, chiefly in mining. James Watt in 1783/84 made a steam engine that was more powerful, more economical in its use of fuel and adapted to operate machinery in factories, and from the 1780s more and more factories adopted steam power.

Railways. Steam power was also applied to land transport in the form of railways. The first modern railway was operated entirely by steam locomotives and carried passengers as well as freight. The Liverpool and Manchester railway was opened in 1830, and by 1850 a network of railways connected all important places in Britain.

Economic results. The basic economic problem in industrial states was no longer the scarcity of commodities but overproduction and the consequent difficulty of selling what was produced. Before the Industrial Revolution, economic depression usually resulted from wars, big epidemics or bad harvests; from the Industrial Revolution onwards a normal cause of depression was overproduction caused by a lack of effective demand. The agricultural sector became less dominant as people transferred to other sectors, but agricultural productivity increased so that fewer people engaged in agriculture produced more food, helped by better methods, artificial fertilisers and pesticides. The shift from the countryside to towns and cities accelerated, and population expanded rapidly in Britain and other industrialised countries of the West despite bad living and working conditions for the working class.

Social and political results. A new class system developed with more class consciousness than ever before. A large industrial capitalist class was added to the existing bourgeoisie of merchants, professional people and bankers, and in the 19th century the bourgeoisie became the economically and politically dominant class, replacing the centuries-long domination of the land-owning nobility. Alongside it grew the new class of the industrial proletariat, more numerous and more concentrated in large factories in towns and cities, and conscious that its interests were antagonistic to those of the bourgeoisie. This proletariat provided the mass base for the new doctrines of socialism and for working class political parties with socialist programmes, and governments and ruling classes were alarmed by the growth of socialism in the 19th century.

Toward imperialism. Industrialisation increased national wealth, although this was very unevenly distributed. From about 1850, industry, technology and science were applied to armies and navies, widening the gap in power between western and non-western states. Western states became more interested in non-western areas as sources of raw materials and as markets, and steamships, railways and the electric telegraph from the 1840s improved transport and communications and tied the world more closely together, so that from the third quarter of the 19th century the world became increasingly one single integrated capitalist world economy. The result of all these changes was the imperialism of the late 19th century, the expanding and accelerated drive for colonial acquisitions and spheres of influence.

Inanimate power generated from burning coal, which became the flexible power source of factories and railways.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the Industrial Revolution first take place in Britain?
workedExamples.given: Coal was cheap and abundant in Britain; the putting out system gave way to large factories; Newcomen built a viable steam engine around 1705/1709 and Watt improved it in 1783/84; the Liverpool and Manchester railway opened in 1830.
workedExamples.formula: Historical analysis: combine natural resources, technological invention and organisation to explain why a change begins where it does.
workedExamples.substitution: Britain had the coal to raise steam, the inventors to build engines and the factory organisation to use them at scale.
workedExamples.calculation: Abundant cheap coal plus practical steam engines plus concentrated factories made cheap mass production possible in Britain earlier than elsewhere.
workedExamples.answer: Because Britain combined cheap abundant coal, working steam engines and the factory system, so cheap mass production began there first.

workedExamples.problem: Explain how the factory system changed the position of the worker compared with the old putting out system.
workedExamples.given: Under the factory system workers owned only their labour power, sold it for money wages, and could be hired and dismissed at the will of the industrial capitalist.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: the separation of the worker from ownership of the means of production.
workedExamples.substitution: The worker no longer worked at home with their own tools but inside a factory owned by someone else.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the capitalist owned the factory and machinery, the worker depended entirely on selling labour by the day for wages.
workedExamples.answer: The worker owned only labour power and became dependent on the wages and hiring decisions of the factory owner.

workedExamples.problem: Before the 18th century bad harvests caused economic depression, but after the Industrial Revolution something else did. Explain the change.
workedExamples.given: Before the Industrial Revolution depression usually resulted from wars, big epidemics or bad harvests; afterwards a normal cause was overproduction caused by a lack of effective demand.
workedExamples.formula: Historical cause and effect: when production is cheap and massive, the problem shifts from shortage to unsold goods.
workedExamples.substitution: Many poor people meant limited demand for the commodities produced.
workedExamples.calculation: Factories could produce more than people could afford to buy, so goods piled up unsold and depression followed from overproduction rather than scarcity.
workedExamples.answer: Depression increasingly came from overproduction caused by a lack of effective demand rather than from war, disease or harvest failure.

workedExamples.problem: Trace how the Industrial Revolution in Britain led to the imperialism of the late 19th century.
workedExamples.given: From about 1850 industry and science were applied to armies and navies; western states wanted raw materials and markets; steamships, railways and the electric telegraph tied the world together.
workedExamples.formula: Historical causation: industrial strength produces military power, which produces colonial expansion.
workedExamples.substitution: A wealthier, better-armed West looked to non-western areas for materials and markets and could enforce its interests.
workedExamples.calculation: Industrial power widened the gap with non-western states and made it easier to resolve conflicts by force, so the drive for colonies accelerated.
workedExamples.answer: Industrial and military power plus the search for raw materials and markets produced the late-19th century imperialism.

commonMistakes: Saying the Industrial Revolution began in France or Germany when the textbook places it in Britain between 1750/1780 and 1850.
Confusing the putting out system, which dispersed work in small units, with the factory system, which concentrated it in large factories.
Crediting James Watt with the first steam engine instead of Newcomen, whose 1705/1709 engine was used mainly for pumps.
Believing industrialisation reduced food output, when fewer farmers actually produced more food through better methods and science.
Thinking overproduction and scarcity are the same problem, when the Industrial Revolution shifted depression towards overproduction from a lack of demand.
Forgetting that the industrial proletariat became the mass base for socialism and working class political parties.
applications: Explaining why a country that can generate cheap power and build factories can produce goods more cheaply than one that cannot.
Debating in class whether the growth of cities during industrialisation improved or harmed ordinary people's lives.
Linking the spread of railways and telegraphs to today's roads, mobile networks and their effect on trade in Ethiopia.
Discussing how an industry such as cotton textiles in Lancashire compares with Ethiopia's growing textile and garment sector.

Explaining how industrial strength can translate into military and diplomatic power in the world today.
g12-history-uh1-t2.summary: The Industrial Revolution was the first establishment of industrial capitalism in any country, and it transformed Britain between 1750/1780 and 1850 through the factory system, steam power and railways. It created cheap mass production and the new problem of overproduction, shrank the dominance of agriculture, accelerated urban growth and produced the industrial bourgeoisie and proletariat. Its wider result was the integration of the world into one capitalist economy and the imperialism of the late 19th century.

g12-history-uh1-t3.overview: Nationalism has been the most powerful political force in the Western world since the 1850s, rooted in shared custom, language and religion. This lesson explains the factors that grew it and how its character changed between the 1880s and 1914.
objectives: Define nationalism and explain its roots in cultural identity
List the major factors that promoted the growth of nationalism
Explain Social Darwinism and its effect on national feeling
Describe how nationalism changed character between the 1880s and 1914
Assess how nationalism contributed to the outbreak of World War I
g12-history-uh1-t3.simple: Nationalism has been the most powerful political force in the Western world since the 1850s. Its deepest roots lie in a shared sense of regional and cultural identity, especially in custom, language and religion, and it influenced the urban population more than rural peasants. Governments promoted it through compulsory primary education and compulsory military service, while cheap newspapers, nationalist literature and patriotic societies spread patriotic and hostile feelings. Wars of unification in Italy and Germany and wars of national liberation in the Balkans stimulated nationalism, and the pseudo-science called Social Darwinism taught that history is a struggle in which the strongest nations win. Between the 1880s and 1914 nationalism turned towards fragmentation, with language and ethnicity as the main criteria, and it helped make World War I possible.
g12-history-uh1-t3.detailed:
The force of nationalism. Nationalism has been the most powerful political force since the 1850s in the Western world. Its deepest roots lie in a shared sense of regional and cultural identity, especially as those roots are expressed in custom, language and religion. It influenced all classes, but more so the urban than the rural peasants.

Nationalism and the road to war. Nationalism created the atmosphere that made World War I possible: it aggravated the great international crisis of 1905-1914 and made the peoples of Europe support the war when it broke out in July-August 1914. Nationalism did not begin in the middle of the nineteenth century, but it grew and intensified from then until World War I.

Schools, armies and the press. Compulsory primary education was used by governments for state building and for inculcating patriotism, and compulsory military service was used to inculcate patriotism and loyalty to the state and its rulers. Cheap newspapers for the masses often had chauvinistic tones, while the quality newspapers for the upper and middle classes also carried nationalism and hostile feelings towards neighbouring states. Much of the literature of the years before World War I was strongly nationalist and warned against the dangers of neighbouring countries, and patriotic societies were created to inculcate patriotism, to agitate for stronger armament and sometimes also for bigger colonial empires.

Wars and pseudo-science. Nationalism was stimulated by the wars of unification in Italy and Germany and by the wars of national liberation in the Balkans. British nationalism was stimulated by the small colonial wars Britain fought so often, though the second Boer War (1899-1902) was an unpleasant shock that cooled British aggressiveness for a time until it was revived by fear of Germany, and in the USA victory in the Spanish-American War of 1898 stimulated American nationalism. Pseudo-science also stimulated nationalism through what became known as Social Darwinism, which spread the idea that history is a struggle between states and nations for power, supremacy and even survival, in which the strongest, and therefore the best, would be the victors while weak states and nations would be subjugated and even destroyed.

Fragmentation after the 1880s. In the period between the 1880s and 1914 nationalism transformed its character. First, more and more national movements appeared in Europe and in the Ottoman Empire outside Europe, many of them among quite small numbers of people living in quite small territories, so that nationalism, which earlier in the nineteenth century had appeared to work towards greater unity as in Italy and Germany, now tended towards fragmentation. Second, language and ethnicity became the major criteria, especially language, and all over Europe submerged minority nationalities struggled to assert the rights of their languages to equality, producing bitter disputes over language questions.

A domestic question and a two-edged weapon. Third, the national question became part of the domestic politics of many states, particularly multinational ones such as Austria-Hungary and Tsarist Russia, and others such as Britain with its serious Irish question. In terms of class, the new minority nationality movements attracted the petty bourgeois, because the success of a national movement and its language would mean not just more prestige for the nationality and its language but more employment in the public sector for the speakers of that language. For a government, nationalism was a two-edged weapon: it could strengthen loyalty to the state and the ruler and divert the workers away from socialism, but where national minorities existed it could also arise from their demands and cause discontent and disloyalty.

Assimilation in the United States. The USA was very successful in the nineteenth century in assimilating millions of emigrants who came to it from Europe. This success was made possible because the migrants left Europe dissatisfied with conditions in their home countries, and by becoming US citizens they joined a country and a nation which offered them more economic opportunities and more social and political freedom.

workedExamples.problem: Using the lesson, explain why nationalism made World War I possible.
workedExamples.given: Nationalism aggravated the great international crisis of 1905-1914 and made the peoples of Europe support the war when it broke out in July-August 1914.
workedExamples.formula: Historical analysis: public sentiment can turn an international crisis into a general war.
workedExamples.substitution: Aggravated rivalry plus popular enthusiasm for war prepared Europe for conflict.
workedExamples.calculation: Since nationalism both sharpened the crisis and won popular backing for war, it created the atmosphere in which the war could begin.
workedExamples.answer: It aggravated the crisis of 1905-1914 and made Europeans support the war, creating the atmosphere for World War I.

workedExamples.problem: Why did nationalism influence the urban population more than rural peasants?
workedExamples.given: Nationalism influenced all classes but more so the urban than the rural peasants, and its carriers included schools, newspapers, literature and patriotic societies.
workedExamples.formula: Historical reasoning: ideas spread fastest where their carriers are concentrated.

workedExamples.problem: Explain what Social Darwinism taught and why it stimulated aggressive nationalism.

workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: pseudo-science used to justify national rivalry and war.

workedExamples.problem: How did nationalism change its character between the 1880s and 1914?

workedExamples.substitution: Earlier unity movements in Italy and Germany gave way to many small minority movements demanding language rights.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the new movements were small and based on language, nationalism now tended to divide states instead of uniting them.

g12-history-uh1-t4.overview: Italian unification joined the separate states of the Italian Peninsula into one nation between the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and the Franco-Prussian War in 1871. This lesson examines the obstacles and favourable factors, the leaders and the stages of the process.
objectives: Define Italian unification and state its beginning and end dates
Describe the political condition of Italy in 1852
Explain why Piedmont took the lead in the movement for unity
Identify the obstacles and favourable factors of Italian unification
Outline the roles of Cavour, Garibaldi and Victor Emmanuel II in the process
g12-history-uh1-t4.simple: Italian unification was the political and social process that united the separate states of the Italian Peninsula into a single nation in the nineteenth century. Most historians say it began with the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and the end of Napoleon's rule and ended with the Franco-Prussian War in 1871. In 1852 Italy was still divided and Austrian influence was supreme, but Piedmont, ruled by King Victor Emmanuel II under a constitution, was independent of Austria and could lead. The main obstacles were the power of Austria and weak national sentiment. Camillo Cavour, prime minister of Piedmont, used an alliance with France to defeat Austria at Magenta and Solferino in 1859, while Giuseppe Garibaldi and his Thousand Volunteers took Naples in 1860. Venetia followed in 1866 and Rome in 1870.
g12-history-uh1-t4.detailed:
The starting point. The political and social process that united the separate states of the Italian Peninsula into a single nation in the nineteenth century is known as Italian unification. It is difficult to put exact dates on its beginning and end, but most historians agree that it began with the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and the end of Napoleon's rule and ended with the Franco-Prussian War in 1871.

Italy divided in 1852. In 1852 Italy was still politically divided and Austrian influence was still supreme. In the north the two rich provinces of Lombardy and Venetia were part of the Austrian Empire. In the north-central part there were the petty states of Parma, Modena and Tuscany, which were very much under Austrian influence and ruled despotically by rulers related to the Hapsburg emperor of Austria. The Papal States still covered a vast territory across Italy, consisting of the Romagna, the Marches, Umbria and Rome and the patrimony, and the pope was both the spiritual head of Catholics all over the world and the sovereign ruler of those states. Since 1849 a French garrison had been in Rome to protect the pope and to show Austria that France had an interest in Italy. The south of Italy and the island of Sicily were part of the kingdom of Naples, which was poor, feudal and backward, ruled despotically, with a king closely allied with Austria. In the northwest was the kingdom of Piedmont, consisting of the mainland territory and the island of Sardinia.

Why Piedmont led. Piedmont was the only Italian state that was really independent of Austria and that had a constitution, a parliament and civil rights, though these had existed only since 1848. This situation made it possible for Piedmont to take the lead in the movement for Italian unification, because liberals and nationalists all over Italy saw their best hope of a united Italy in unification with Piedmont under the constitutional monarchy of King Victor Emmanuel II (r.1849-1878).

Obstacles and favourable factors. The main obstacle to Italian political unification was the power of Austria, which wanted to maintain the status quo, and another obstacle was the weakness of national sentiment in Italy. A favourable factor in the struggle for unification was the diplomatic isolation of Austria after the Crimean War (1855-56) and the rivalries between France and Austria in Italy, which meant that Italian nationalism was able to use French help for Italian aims.

Cavour and the war with Austria. Camillo Cavour (1810-61), prime minister of Piedmont from 1852 to 1862, was the main architect of Italian unification from above and prepared Piedmont for the role of leadership. In 1858 Cavour met the French emperor Napoleon III secretly at Plombieres in France and reached an agreement for an alliance of France and Piedmont against Austria. In April 1859 Cavour successfully provoked a declaration of war by Austria on Piedmont, and Napoleon III intervened on the side of Piedmont. The combined force invaded Lombardy and defeated the Austrian army at the Battles of Magenta and Solferino in June 1859, driving the Austrians out of Lombardy although they still held Venetia, and one result of the Battle of Solferino was the establishment of the International Red Cross Association by the Swiss humanitarian Henri Dunant. Napoleon, however, concluded a unilateral peace treaty with Austria on the basis that Austria ceded Lombardy to Piedmont but kept Venetia.

Garibaldi and the south. The papal province of Romagna and the states of Parma, Modena and Tuscany revolted against their rulers in 1859, their rulers were overthrown, and provisional governments were established which demanded union with Piedmont. Once the north had been united as the Kingdom of Italy, the unification movement turned to absorbing the powerful Kingdom of Two Sicilies in the south. In 1860 there was an uprising in Sicily against the unpopular government of the Kingdom of Naples, and the successful military leader Garibaldi was invited from Piedmont to lead it. He agreed provided that the people accepted the programme of unification with the rest of Italy under Victor Emmanuel; he recruited his famous Thousand Volunteers in the North, took them to Sicily, was joined by other volunteers, advanced up the peninsula and took the city of Naples on September 7, 1860. Garibaldi succeeded because of his skill as a leader in guerrilla warfare and his magnetic personality, because he mobilized the Sicilian masses who hoped his movement would bring freedom from oppression, and because on the mainland the army of Naples was demoralized and many of its officials were defeatist or treacherous.

Completion. The fall of Gaeta brought the unification movement to a successful conclusion, leaving only Rome and Venetia to be added. On February 18, 1861, Victor Emmanuel assembled the deputies of all the states that acknowledged his supremacy at Turin and assumed the title of King of Italy, and four months later Cavour died. The Italian government then used the 1866 Austro-Prussian War and the 1870-71 Franco-Prussian War to complete unification: in 1866 Bismarck made an alliance with Italy on the basis that Italy would fight Austria and receive Venetia, and Prussia's success forced Austria to cede Venetia; in 1870 the Franco-Prussian War forced Napoleon III to withdraw French troops from Rome, so Italian troops seized Rome in September 1870 and it soon became the capital of Italy.

workedExamples.problem: Why did Piedmont, rather than any other Italian state, lead the movement for unification?
workedExamples.given: Piedmont was the only Italian state really independent of Austria and had a constitution, a parliament and civil rights since 1848, under King Victor Emmanuel II (r.1849-1878).
workedExamples.formula: Historical analysis: leadership passes to the state that already has independence and liberal institutions.
workedExamples.substitution: Other states were under Austrian influence or despotically ruled, while Piedmont had independence and a constitution.
workedExamples.calculation: Because liberals and nationalists wanted a united Italy with a constitution, Piedmont was the only realistic leader.
workedExamples.answer: Because it alone was independent of Austria and had a constitution, a parliament and civil rights.

workedExamples.problem: What were the main obstacles and the main favourable factor in Italian unification?
workedExamples.given: The power of Austria, which wanted the status quo, and the weakness of national sentiment were obstacles, while the diplomatic isolation of Austria after the Crimean War (1855-56) and Franco-Austrian rivalry were favourable.
workedExamples.formula: Historical skill: sorting evidence into obstacles and favourable factors.
workedExamples.substitution: Austrian power blocked unity, but Austria's isolation after the Crimean War let Italy use French help.
workedExamples.calculation: By allying with France against an isolated Austria, Italy turned its main obstacle into a manageable one.
workedExamples.answer: The obstacles were Austria's power and weak national sentiment; the favourable factor was Austria's isolation and Franco-Austrian rivalry, which let Italy use French help.

workedExamples.problem: How did Garibaldi's expedition of 1860 help unite Italy, and why did Cavour stop it?
workedExamples.given: Garibaldi recruited the Thousand Volunteers and took Naples on September 7, 1860, and Cavour stopped his advance at the River Volturno in September 1860, completing the defeat of the king of Naples with the army of Piedmont.
workedExamples.formula: Historical analysis: a revolutionary success can threaten the political aims of a cautious statesman.
workedExamples.substitution: Garibaldi's volunteers could have marched on Rome and provoked France, while Cavour wanted a monarchy-led union under Victor Emmanuel.
workedExamples.calculation: Stopping Garibaldi at the Volturno kept the movement under Piedmont's control and avoided a clash with France.
workedExamples.answer: Garibaldi's campaign won the south for Italy, and Cavour stopped it at the Volturno so that Piedmont and diplomacy, not a revolutionary advance, would complete the union.

workedExamples.problem: Explain how the completion of Italian unification in 1866 and 1870 depended on other wars.
workedExamples.given: In 1866 Bismarck allied with Italy against Austria and Prussia's success forced Austria to cede Venetia; in 1870 the Franco-Prussian War forced Napoleon III to withdraw French troops from Rome, which Italian troops then seized in September 1870.
workedExamples.formula: Historical causation: unification advanced when great-power wars removed foreign protection from Italian territories.
workedExamples.substitution: Austria held Venetia and France protected Rome, so only defeats of those powers could free the territories.
workedExamples.calculation: Prussia's victories removed both obstacles, so Venetia was gained in 1866 and Rome in 1870.
workedExamples.answer: Because Prussia's wars defeated Austria and France, the two powers that held Venetia and protected Rome, Italy could complete unification.

Claiming the French garrison in Rome helped Italy, when it protected the pope and was withdrawn only in 1870.
Mixing up the 1859 Battles of Magenta and Solferino with the seizure of Rome in 1870.

g12-history-uh1-t5.overview: In the 1850s Germany was a loose confederation of 39 states, the Bund, presided over by Austria. This lesson explains the obstacles to unity and the three wars through which Bismarck's Prussia created the German Empire in 1871.
objectives: Describe the German Confederation and the demand for real political unity
Identify the obstacles to German unification
Explain Bismarck's appointment and his method of overcoming the army crisis
Outline Bismarck's three military successes
Compare the unification of Italy with the unification of Germany
g12-history-uh1-t5.simple: In the 1850s Germany was a loose confederation of 39 states called the German Confederation, or the Bund, presided over by Austria with Prussia second. German nationalists wanted real political unity, and their cause was encouraged by Italy's unification between 1859 and 1861. The obstacles were Austria, the German princes who wanted to keep their independence, and the cultural differences between North and South Germany. In 1861 William I became King of Prussia and appointed Otto von Bismarck as chief minister. Bismarck united Germany through three military successes: defeating Denmark in 1864 and gaining Schleswig-Holstein, defeating Austria at Koniggratz in 1866, and defeating France in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-71, after which Wilhelm I was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles.
g12-history-uh1-t5.detailed:
The German Confederation. In the 1850s Germany was a loose confederation of 39 states called the German Confederation, or the Bund. The Bund was presided over by Austria, with Prussia second. It was not a satisfactory form of unity for German nationalists, who wanted real political unity for reasons of German nationalism and for economic reasons, and German nationalism was encouraged by the success of Italian national unification between 1859 and 1861.

Obstacles. The obstacles to German unification were Austria, which wanted to preserve the status quo; the German princes, who wanted to keep their independence; and the cultural differences between North and South Germany.

The army crisis and Bismarck. In 1861 William I (r.1861-1888) was crowned King of Prussia. He and his war minister Von Roon proposed enlarging and reforming the Prussian army to give Prussia more influence against Austria and security against France, but the proposal was opposed by the Prussian parliament, which refused to vote the necessary new taxation, and an important issue behind the dispute was who would control the army. The king therefore appointed Otto von Bismarck as chief minister of Prussia. Bismarck (1815-1898) was politically conservative but a political realist and extremely able, and he soon overcame the crisis by collecting additional taxation for the army reforms without the consent of parliament; there was no resistance. German nationalism rapidly shifted from its liberal and democratic character in 1848 to Bismarck's authoritarian rule.

Bismarck's assessment. Bismarck knew that Germany could not be united under Prussia without war against Austria and probably France. Austria would not give up its leadership in the Bund unless it suffered a defeat, and the traditional French policy was to keep Germany politically divided and therefore weak, so France too would probably not accept German unification unless it suffered a military defeat. Bismarck also knew that his programme would not be possible without good relations between Prussia and Russia, so he exerted all his diplomatic skills to maintain them; he was helped by the fact that Prussia and Russia had a common interest in opposing Polish nationalism, and during the great Polish revolt of 1863 Prussia was the only great power that was sympathetic to Russia.

The three wars. Bismarck accomplished unification through three military successes. He first allied with Austria to defeat Denmark in a short war fought in 1864, thus acquiring Schleswig-Holstein. In 1866, with the support of Italy, he virtually created the Austro-Prussian War and won a decisive victory at the Battle of Koniggratz, which allowed him to exclude the long-time rival Austria when forming the North German Confederation with the states that had supported Prussia, and that Confederation was the direct precursor of the 1871 Empire. Finally, Prussia defeated France in the Franco-Prussian War (1870-71), and the German Confederation was transformed into an Empire with the proclamation of the Prussian King Wilhelm I as German Emperor at the Palace of Versailles, to the humiliation of France.

Comparing Italy and Germany. Both unifications were achieved by war and diplomacy, but Cavour's Piedmont depended heavily on the help of France, while Bismarck's Prussia was strong enough to act as the leading power and to use Austria in one war and Italy in another. In Italy Victor Emmanuel II became King of Italy in 1861, whereas in Germany the Prussian king Wilhelm I was proclaimed German Emperor only in 1871 at Versailles.

workedExamples.problem: Analyse the strategies Bismarck used to unite Germany.
workedExamples.given: Bismarck collected extra taxation without parliament's consent, kept good relations with Russia, allied with Austria against Denmark in 1864, with Italy against Austria in 1866, and defeated France in 1870-71.
workedExamples.formula: Historical analysis: combine domestic strength, diplomacy and war to isolate enemies one at a time.
workedExamples.substitution: He secured Russia's goodwill and won allies for each war so that his main opponents could be defeated separately.
workedExamples.calculation: By fighting Denmark, then Austria, then France in sequence he never faced them all at once, and each victory removed the next obstacle to unity.
workedExamples.answer: Bismarck used authoritarian taxation for army reform, diplomacy to befriend Russia, and three separate wars to defeat Denmark, Austria and France one after another.

workedExamples.problem: Why did Bismarck believe Germany could not be united without war against Austria and probably France?
workedExamples.given: Austria would not give up its leadership in the Bund unless defeated, and traditional French policy was to keep Germany politically divided and weak.
workedExamples.formula: Historical analysis: work out an aim from the known interests of the opposing powers.
workedExamples.substitution: Austria blocked unity by constitutional means and France blocked it by preferring a divided Germany.
workedExamples.calculation: Since neither power would accept unity voluntarily, only defeat could remove their opposition.
workedExamples.answer: Because Austria would keep its leadership and France wanted a divided Germany unless both were defeated in war.

workedExamples.problem: What did the North German Confederation show about the character of German nationalism after 1866?
workedExamples.given: After the victory at Koniggratz, Prussia formed the North German Confederation with the states that had supported it, and German nationalism had shifted from its liberal and democratic character in 1848 to Bismarck's authoritarian rule.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: the same national aim can be carried out under very different political systems.
workedExamples.substitution: Unity was now being built by a powerful conservative state rather than by liberal popular movements.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the Confederation was created by Prussia after a war and not by a liberal assembly, it shows nationalism serving authoritarian rule.
workedExamples.answer: It shows that German nationalism had shifted from a liberal and democratic movement to Bismarck's authoritarian rule.

workedExamples.problem: Compare the roles of France in the unification of Italy and of Austria in the unification of Germany.
workedExamples.given: Cavour allied with France against Austria, and Napoleon III's help won Lombardy in 1859; Bismarck allied with Austria against Denmark in 1864 and then defeated Austria in 1866.
workedExamples.formula: Historical comparison: the same type of power can be an ally in one case and an obstacle in another.
workedExamples.substitution: France helped Piedmont achieve Italian aims, while Austria was Germany's rival for leadership of the Bund.
workedExamples.calculation: Italy used France against Austria, but Prussia used Austria for one war and then removed it as a rival in the next.
workedExamples.answer: France was a useful ally for Italy, whereas Austria was briefly Prussia's ally and then the rival that had to be defeated.

g12-history-uh1-t6.overview: The American Civil War was fought from 1861 to 1865 between the northern states of the Union and the seceding southern Confederacy. This lesson examines the divisive issues, the election of Lincoln, the Emancipation Proclamation and the results of the war.
objectives: Outline the divisive issues between the North and the South
Explain how slavery outweighed all other issues
Describe the role of Abraham Lincoln and the Republican Party
Explain the Emancipation Proclamation and why the Union prevailed
Assess the results of the Civil War, including the three amendments
g12-history-uh1-t6.simple: The American Civil War was fought in the United States from 1861 to 1865 between the forces of the 23 northern states of the Union and the newly formed Confederate States of America, made up of 11 southern states that had declared secession. The main divisive issues were economic dominance, tariffs, states' rights against the federal government, and above all slavery, which outweighed all other issues and was the only one capable of producing secession and civil war. The Republican Party was founded in 1854 and opposed the expansion of slavery; in 1860 the election of Abraham Lincoln triggered secession, and seven states formed the Confederacy on February 9, 1861. Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation in September 1862, effective January 1, 1863. The North won in April 1865 and the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery.
g12-history-uh1-t6.detailed:
What the war was. The American Civil War was fought in the United States from 1861 until 1865 between the forces coming mostly from the 23 northern states of the Union and the newly formed Confederate States of America, which consisted of 11 southern states that had declared their secession.

Divisive issues. There were several divisive issues between the North and the South. The South resented the economic dominance of the North. The South wanted low tariffs to ensure cheaper imports from Europe, while the North wanted protective tariffs to encourage its industries. The South emphasised states' rights, the constitutional rights of the individual states, while the North put more emphasis on the national federal government. However, the slavery issue outweighed all other issues and was the only issue capable of producing secession and civil war, and when the South lost control of the political institutions of the USA it turned to secession, fearing that northern domination of the Union would lead to attacks on slavery.

Tensions in the 1850s. Tensions grew rapidly during the 1850s. The United States Republican Party was established in 1854, and the new party opposed the expansion of slavery in the western territories, mobilising popular support among Northerners and Westerners who did not want to compete against slave labour. The year 1860 was a year of presidential election, and at that time the Republican Party had a very good candidate named Abraham Lincoln, who was an effective politician, an able speaker and an attractive personality, a man who appealed to ordinary northerners because he was self-educated. In 1860 Lincoln's election as President triggered secession in the South, as the South had warned before the elections, because his election was seen as an intolerable threat to slavery.

Secession and the outbreak of war. Before Lincoln took office, seven states seceded from the Union, establishing a rebel government known as the Confederate States of America on February 9, 1861, and they took control of federal forts and property within their boundaries. On March 4, 1861, Abraham Lincoln was sworn in as President of the United States, and in his inaugural address he called secession legally void. He stated that he had no intent to invade the southern states but would use force to maintain possession of federal property, and he then called for all the states in the Union to send troops to recapture the forts and preserve the Union.

The war and its results. The northerners were willing to fight to end secession, and though the North initially fought to end secession and not to end slavery, slavery had caused secession, so the causes of the war were both slavery and secession. The North had most of the advantages: more states, a much bigger population, more skilled labour, far more industry, more railways, much greater agricultural production except for cotton, much greater financial wealth and naval power to block the South and cut off essential imports. Although the British and French governments and ruling classes sympathised with the South's king cotton, they were not strong enough to intervene on its side. The North did not win easily, because the South had initially better generals, fought with great determination, and the defensive power of firearms favoured it; the war lasted from 1861 to 1865 and claimed the lives of 620,000 people. In September 1862 Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation to become effective as of January 1, 1863, declaring that all slaves in rebel-held territory would be free from that date; it helped the North recruit African American troops, many of whom served with distinction, and it damaged the South by encouraging slaves to run away from the plantations, especially when the northern army advanced.

End and consequences. In April 1865 the Confederacy was finally defeated unconditionally and completely, and a few days later, on April 14, 1865, Lincoln was assassinated by a southern fanatic named John Wilkes Booth. The civil war decided once and for all the issues of secession and slavery, and both ended with the victory of the North. After the war southern political leaders had virtually no impact on the immediate post-war decisions, and several amendments to the US constitution were made: the Thirteenth abolished slavery, the Fourteenth granted citizenship to former slaves, and the Fifteenth allowed them to vote.

workedExamples.formula: Historical skill: rank causes by their capacity to produce the event.
workedExamples.substitution: Economic rivalry, tariffs and states' rights divided the sections, but slavery was the only issue capable of producing secession and war.
workedExamples.calculation: Because only slavery could drive the South to leave the Union, it is the decisive cause, with the others as underlying divisions.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the North's advantages not produce an easy victory?

workedExamples.formula: Historical analysis: material superiority does not by itself guarantee a quick victory.
workedExamples.substitution: The South fought on the defensive with better commanders, which offset much of the North's material lead.

workedExamples.substitution: Making the war a struggle against slavery gained soldiers and made it politically and morally impossible for European governments to support the Confederacy.
workedExamples.calculation: The proclamation therefore strengthened the northern armies and closed off European intervention at the same time.
workedExamples.answer: It recruited African American troops and weakened the South's labour force, while making European support for the Confederacy impossible.

workedExamples.problem: What did the Civil War decide, and how did the constitution express that outcome?

workedExamples.formula: Historical skill: connect a war's outcome to the legal changes that follow it.
workedExamples.substitution: Northern victory ended secession and slavery, and the amendments wrote these results into the constitution.
workedExamples.calculation: Abolition, citizenship and the vote for former slaves follow logically from the North's defeat of secession and slavery.
workedExamples.answer: It settled secession and slavery in favour of the North, and the Thirteenth abolished slavery, the Fourteenth gave citizenship to former slaves and the Fifteenth gave them the vote.

g12-history-uh1-t7.overview: The Eastern Question was the problem of what would happen to the Ottoman Empire in the Balkans and elsewhere as Ottoman power declined. This lesson covers great-power rivalry, the treaties of San Stefano and Berlin, and the Balkan Wars of 1912-1913.
objectives: Explain what the Eastern Question meant and why it mattered
Describe the interests of Russia, Austria-Hungary and Britain in the Balkans
Outline the terms of the Treaties of San Stefano and Berlin
Explain the causes and results of the two Balkan Wars
Trace how the Eastern Question contributed to the outbreak of World War I
g12-history-uh1-t7.simple: The Eastern Question was the problem of what would happen to the Ottoman Empire in the Balkans and elsewhere as Ottoman power declined. In the Balkans the empire was threatened by Balkan national movements usually backed by Russia, and its decline benefited Russia, while Austria-Hungary and the United Kingdom demanded that the empire be preserved. In April 1877 Russia declared war on the Ottoman Empire and imposed the Treaty of San Stefano on March 3, 1878, which the Great Powers then revised at the Treaty of Berlin on July 13, 1878. Austria-Hungary later annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908, and the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913 stripped the Ottoman Empire of almost all its remaining European territory. The tension between Austria-Hungary and Serbia, worsened by the assassination of Franz Ferdinand in 1914, led to the First World War.
g12-history-uh1-t7.detailed:
What the Eastern Question meant. The Eastern Question meant what would happen to the Ottoman Empire in the Balkans and elsewhere as Ottoman power declined. In the Balkans the Ottoman Empire was threatened by the militancy of Balkan national movements, backed usually by Russia, and the Eastern Question was an issue of political and economic instability in the Ottoman Empire from the late 18th to the early 20th centuries. It was also the main cause of the subsequent strategic competition and political considerations of the European great powers in the region.

Great-power rivalry. As the collapse of the Ottoman Empire approached, the European powers engaged in a power struggle to safeguard their military, strategic and commercial interests in the Ottoman domains. The decline of the Ottoman Empire benefited Imperial Russia, while on the other hand Austria-Hungary and the United Kingdom demanded the Empire's preservation as being in their best interests.

War and the first two treaties. In the 1870s the hardships of the Ottomans increased, their treasury was empty, and they faced insurrections not only in Herzegovina and Bulgaria but also in Serbia and Montenegro, although the Ottoman Empire managed to crush the insurgents in August 1876. Russia now intended to enter the conflict on the side of the rebels, using rumours of Ottoman atrocities against the rebellious population as an excuse, and in April 1877 Russia declared war against the Ottoman Empire. It had effectively secured Austrian neutrality with the Reichstadt Agreement of July 1876, under which Ottoman territories captured during the war would be partitioned between the Russian and Austria-Hungarian Empires, the latter obtaining Bosnia and Herzegovina. Britain did not involve itself at first, but when Russia threatened to conquer Constantinople, now Istanbul, Britain urged Austria and Germany to ally with it against Russia. Russia negotiated peace through the Treaty of San Stefano of 3 March 1878, which stipulated independence for Romania, Serbia and Montenegro; autonomy for Bulgaria; reforms in Bosnia and Herzegovina; the ceding of Dobruja and parts of Armenia; and a large indemnity to Russia, which would give Russia great influence in Southeastern Europe.

The Treaty of Berlin. To reduce these advantages to Russia, the Great Powers, especially Britain, insisted on a thorough revision of the Treaty of San Stefano. At the Treaty of Berlin on July 13, 1878, the boundaries of the new states were adjusted in the Ottoman Empire's favour. Bulgaria was divided into two states, Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia, because it was feared that a single state would be susceptible to Russian domination, and Bosnia and Herzegovina were transferred to Austrian control. Later, Austria-Hungary took advantage of the Ottoman crisis to annex the two provinces in 1908, an act that outraged Pan-Slav nationalists in Serbia, who had long anticipated a merger with Bosnia in a union of the southern Slavs, and this eventually became an immediate cause of World War I.

Alliances and the Balkan Wars. Germany drew away from Russia and became closer to Austria-Hungary, with whom it concluded the Dual Alliance in 1879, and Germany was also closely allied with the Ottoman Empire, taking over the reorganisation of the Ottoman military and financial systems and receiving commercial concessions including permission to build the Baghdad Railway. Britain agreed the Entente Cordiale with France in 1904 and made peace with Russia in 1907 through the Anglo-Russian Entente. The Balkan Wars were two successive military conflicts in the Balkan Peninsula in 1912 and 1913 that deprived the Ottoman Empire of all its remaining territory in Europe except part of Thrace and the city of Adrianople. The First Balkan War began on October 8, 1912, when Serbia, Montenegro, Bulgaria and Greece, who had formed the Balkan League in 1912 with Russian support to take Macedonia away from Turkey, attacked the Ottoman Empire; the allies were soon victorious, an armistice was signed on December 3, 1912, and after a coup d'etat by the Young Turks in Constantinople in January 1913 the war continued, with Ioannina falling to the Greeks and Adrianople to the Bulgarians. Under a peace treaty signed in London on May 30, 1913, the Ottoman Empire lost almost all of its remaining European territory, including all of Macedonia and Albania, and Albanian independence was insisted upon by the European powers.

The Second Balkan War and the road to 1914. The Second Balkan War erupted when the allies Serbia, Greece and Bulgaria quarrelled among themselves over the partitioning of their conquests in Macedonia. Bulgaria faced Serbia and Greece, who were joined by Romania, and the war began on the night of June 29-30, 1913, when King Ferdinand of Bulgaria ordered his troops to attack Serbian and Greek forces in Macedonia; the Ottoman Empire also attacked Bulgaria and advanced in Thrace, regaining Adrianople. On July 30 an armistice ended hostilities, and the Treaty of Bucharest was signed on August 10, 1913, under which Greece and Serbia divided most of Macedonia between themselves, leaving Bulgaria with only a small part. The Balkan Wars were marked by ethnic cleansing, with all parties responsible for grave atrocities against civilians. As a result, Greece gained southern Macedonia and the island of Crete, Serbia gained the Kosovo region and extended into northern and central Macedonia, and Albania was made an independent state by a German prince. The most alarming aspect was the growth of tension between Austria-Hungary and Serbia: having obtained an assurance of German support, Austria-Hungary delivered an ultimatum on October 17, 1913, to force Serbia to withdraw from the Albanian borderlands, and the conflict was aggravated by the assassination of the Austrian prince Franz Ferdinand by a Serb nationalist named Gavrilo Princip on June 28, 1914, in Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia. This convinced Austro-Hungary to attack Serbia, and the invasion of Serbia by Austria-Hungary led to the First World War.

workedExamples.problem: What were the motives behind Russian ambitions in the Balkans?
workedExamples.given: In the Balkans the Ottoman Empire was threatened by national movements backed usually by Russia; the decline of the Ottoman Empire benefited Imperial Russia, which secured Austrian neutrality by the Reichstadt Agreement and imposed the Treaty of San Stefano.
workedExamples.formula: Historical analysis: connect a power's ambitions to its gain from another's decline.
workedExamples.substitution: As Ottoman power fell, Russia could extend its influence over the new states and gain territory and an indemnity.
workedExamples.calculation: The Treaty of San Stefano gave Russia influence by making Romania, Serbia and Montenegro independent, giving Bulgaria autonomy and gaining Dobruja and parts of Armenia, so Russia's motive was influence and territory at Ottoman expense.
workedExamples.answer: Russia wanted to profit from Ottoman decline by extending its influence over the Balkans and gaining territory, an indemnity and control over newly independent states.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the Great Powers revise the Treaty of San Stefano at Berlin?
workedExamples.given: San Stefano would give Russia great influence in Southeastern Europe, and the Great Powers, especially Britain, insisted on a thorough revision.
workedExamples.formula: Historical analysis: rival powers act to prevent one state from gaining a decisive advantage.
workedExamples.substitution: A settlement that let Russia dominate the new states was unacceptable to Britain and Austria-Hungary.
workedExamples.calculation: At Berlin the boundaries were adjusted in the Ottoman Empire's favour, Bulgaria was divided into two, and Bosnia and Herzegovina went to Austria, all of which cut back Russian gains.
workedExamples.answer: Because the settlement would have made Russia dominant in Southeastern Europe, so the powers revised it to reduce Russian advantages.

workedExamples.problem: Explain the causes and results of the two Balkan Wars.
workedExamples.given: In 1912 Serbia, Montenegro, Bulgaria and Greece formed the Balkan League with Russian support to take Macedonia from Turkey; the Second War erupted when the allies quarrelled over partitioning their conquests.
workedExamples.formula: Historical causation: a victorious alliance can fall apart over the division of what it has won.
workedExamples.substitution: The first war was fought to drive the Ottomans from Europe, and the second over how the captured lands should be shared.
workedExamples.calculation: Victory removed the common enemy, so the allies turned on each other; the results were the Ottoman loss of nearly all European territory, Greek and Serbian gains, an independent Albania, and heightened Austro-Serbian tension.
workedExamples.answer: The first war was caused by the Balkan League's wish to take Macedonia from the Ottomans and the second by a quarrel over dividing the conquests; the results were Ottoman losses, Greek and Serbian gains, an independent Albania and greater Austro-Serbian hostility.

workedExamples.problem: Trace how the Eastern Question led to the First World War.
workedExamples.given: Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908, delivered an ultimatum to Serbia on October 17, 1913, and Franz Ferdinand was assassinated by Gavrilo Princip in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914.
workedExamples.formula: Historical causation: a chain of Balkan crises between rival powers produced the general war.
workedExamples.substitution: Austrian annexation and the ultimatum angered Serbia, and the assassination gave Austria-Hungary the occasion to attack Serbia.
workedExamples.calculation: Each step increased Austro-Serbian tension until the assassination convinced Austria-Hungary that crushing Serbia was the only solution, and its invasion of Serbia triggered the wider war.
workedExamples.answer: Austrian annexation of Bosnia, the ultimatum to Serbia and the assassination of Franz Ferdinand raised Austro-Serbian tension until the invasion of Serbia led to the First World War.

commonMistakes: Thinking the Eastern Question was only about the Ottoman Empire in the Balkans, when it also concerned Ottoman domains elsewhere.
Believing all the Great Powers wanted the Ottoman Empire to collapse, when Austria-Hungary and Britain demanded its preservation.
Confusing the Treaty of San Stefano (3 March 1878), which favoured Russia, with the Treaty of Berlin (13 July 1878), which cut back Russian gains.
Forgetting that Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina only in 1908, long after the Treaty of Berlin transferred them to its control.
Mixing up the First Balkan War (from October 8, 1912) with the Second Balkan War (from June 29-30, 1913).
Assuming the Balkan Wars were fought only against the Ottomans, when the second was fought among the former allies over Macedonia.
applications: Explaining how the decline of one empire can draw several great powers into rivalry over its territory.

g12-history-uh1-t7.summary: The Eastern Question was what would happen to the Ottoman Empire in the Balkans and elsewhere as Ottoman power declined, and it made the region a focus of great-power rivalry. Russia advanced its influence, Austria-Hungary and Britain sought to preserve the Empire, and the treaties of San Stefano in March 1878 and Berlin in July 1878 settled and then revised the terms. The Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913 stripped the Ottoman Empire of nearly all its European territory, and the deepening conflict between Austria-Hungary and Serbia, culminating in the assassination of Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in 1914, led to the First World War.
